papers.title: Effects of modelling choices on early invasive risk assessments: lessons from the psyllid vectors of Citrus Huanglongbing
papers.authors: Pedro Nunes, Virginie Ravigné, Nicolas Sauvion, Christine N. Meynard
papers.abstract: Abstract Species distribution models (SDMs) are widely used in early invasion risk assessments and are increasingly critical for anticipating biological threats under global change. Yet, SDM outcomes can vary substantially depending on modelling choices, many of which remain poorly standardized. These variations have tangible consequences when model outputs guide regulatory and management decisions. Here, we systematically evaluated how five key modelling decisions affect the performance and spatial projections of early-stage invasion risk models, including strategies that reflect the most common practices: (i) quality and curation of occurrence data, (ii) use of native-only versus native and invasion occurrence data in model calibration, (iii) background point selection, (iv) environmental variable selection, and (v) ensemble versus single-model approaches. In addition to conventional whole-range evaluation metrics (AUC, TSS, Boyce index), we applied a complementary index focused on the invaded range: the invasive False Negative Rate (iFNR). papers.title: Mapping long-distance jump dispersal risk by leveraging transport infrastructure data and sampling bias correction: a case study with the invasive spotted lanternfly (Lycorma delicatula)
papers.authors: Joseph A. Keller, Nadège Bélouard, Sebastiano De Bona, Jocelyn E. Behm, Matthew R. Helmus
papers.abstract: Long-distance jump dispersal accelerates invasive species spread. Analysis of past jumps can identify invasion pathways and point to locations at risk of future colonization, but spatial bias in survey records obscures patterns. To inform surveillance for the spreading invasive grape pest Lycorma delicatula (Hemiptera: Fulgoridae), we gathered 82,890 agency records of established invasive populations from the United States. We used a clustering algorithm to identify 207 jump dispersal sites, and we developed a bias-aware comparison dataset by filtering records to identify proactive search effort at locations not yet known to hold L. delicatula. We measured points' proximity to a co-produced list of 22 property types encompassing categories with high vehicle traffic, railroads, and related contexts that may transport L. delicatula. Bootstrapping analysis showed that proactive surveys were concentrated near hypothesized influential property types, confirming substantial sampling bias. With this bias accounted for, historical jump dispersal sites were closer than expected to 15 property types, particularly distribution centers, truck rentals, flea markets, and importers. papers.title: Climate-Based Modeling of Invasive Species Impact on Urban Green Infrastructure Using CLIMEX and Remote Sensing Data
papers.authors: A. Suresh kumar, C. Rajan
papers.source: OpenAlex / Journal of Smart Infrastructure and Environmental Sustainability
papers.abstract: The pace at which invasive alien species are established and spread is becoming a threat, especially to urban ecosystems, due, in part, to the variability of climates, urban growth, and fragmentation of habitats. These biological invasions are highly dangerous to urban green infrastructure (UGI), which sabotages biodiversity, ecological services, and ecological resilience in the long term. A unravelled modelling approach to employ the CLIMEX model of species distribution as well as the spatial analysis of ecosystems via remote sensing to observe invasion risk zones and map them in the fast urbanising landscapes was created in this work. The climatic suitability of chosen invasive species in the current and future climate conditions under parameters serving as temperature, precipitation, and humidity was simulated with the help of the CLIMEX model, and the land cover dynamics and vegetation indices (as well as the urban heat islands) were measured with the assistance of remote sensing data (Sentinel-2 and ModiS) measurements. papers.title: The ecological adaptability of pinewood nematode populations: survival strategies, mechanisms and co‐evolution
papers.authors: Chen‐Xi Ying, Tong‐Yue Wen, Xiao‐Lei Ding, Xiao‐Qin Wu
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Bursaphelenchus xylophilus (pinewood nematode, PWN) is the causal agent of pine wilt disease and ranks among the most destructive invasive pests threatening global forest ecosystems. Since its introduction to China, this nematode has triggered massive ecological and economic losses, while its distribution range continues to expand northward. The association between the widespread dispersal of B. xylophilus in invaded areas and the ecological adaptability of its populations has drawn considerable attention. RESULTS: This review systematically synthesizes recent research advances regarding the ecological adaptability of PWN populations, elaborating on molecular mechanisms and ecological strategies that enable the nematode to colonize novel environments. In terms of thermal adaptation, differentially expressed genes, small heat shock protein families and the accumulation of key metabolites collectively shape adaptive pathways to resist extreme high and low temperature stress. For host adaptation, PWN displays polyphagous feeding habits and relies on diverse arboreal fungi as nutritional resources when pines were weakened or died. papers.title: Realization and analysis of Artificial Intelligence appearance in Agricultural system
papers.authors: Divya Verma, Kalpna suman, Sachin Pachauri, Baljeet Yadav, Gaurav Verma
papers.source: OpenAlex / International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology
papers.abstract: Agriculture is increasingly expected to produce more food while minimizing the usage of water, chemical-based fertilizers, energy, chemicals, and labor. Agricultural decision-making is further complicated by climate unpredictability, soil degradation, shortages of water, crop illnesses, pests, weeds, and yield uncertainties. An IEEE-style review and implementation methodology for AI in agriculture is presented in this research. Examined are a number of important applications, including as crop recommendations, crop-yield estimation, disease and pest recognition, weed identification, soil and nutrient administration, smart irrigating, weather forecasting, livestock monitoring, agricultural robots, and post-harvest management. A multilayer AI-enabled farming system is proposed in which a conventional sensor, image processing, and historical information are acquired through IoT, UAV, satellites, and field devices; processed information is provided to machine-learning(ML)/deep-learning models; and the ensuing decisions are transmitted to farmers or automated actuators. papers.title: Brown Planthopper (Nilaparvata lugens Stål): Biology, Ecology, Climate Change and Integrated Pest Management in Rice
papers.authors: K Suresh Kumar, Devi Pratyusha D., Madhu U., Sneha R, Gopu Sushma
papers.source: OpenAlex / Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Abstract: The brown planthopper (BPH), Nilaparvata lugens Stål, is one of the most destructive pests of irrigated rice in Asia, causing yield losses of 10–30% under moderate infestations and up to complete crop failure during severe outbreaks. This chapter reviews its taxonomy, biology, host range, and damage mechanisms, including direct phloem feeding leading to "hopper burn" and indirect losses from transmitting Rice Ragged Stunt and Rice Grassy Stunt viruses. High reproductive potential, migratory wing dimorphism, and growing insecticide resistance make BPH management increasingly difficult. The chapter also examines how climate change via rising temperatures, elevated CO₂, and shifting rainfall is intensifying outbreaks and expanding its range, and discusses natural enemies, economic threshold levels, and an integrated pest management strategy combining resistant varieties, cultural, biological, and judicious chemical control for sustainable rice production.

papers.authors: Xiaoxue Ma, Hanqi Xie, Qunfang Huang, Yang E. Hong, Jinmeng Zhang
papers.abstract: The invasion and spread of alien aquatic organisms pose an increasing threat to ecosystem stability and functioning, biodiversity conservation, and socioeconomic development under ongoing climate change. However, limited attention has been given to the compound ecological risks of multi-species invasions driven by the combined effects of climate factors, topography, water quality, vegetation, and other environmental variables under future climate scenarios. Focusing on Pomacea canaliculata (P. canaliculata) and Pontederia crassipes ( P. crassipes ), this study employed the MaxEnt model and spatial analysis to identify key environmental determinants and to project current and future habitat suitability in the middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River Basin under SSP245 and SSP585 scenarios. The results show that the MaxEnt model performed with high accuracy for P. crassipes (AUC = 0.954) and good accuracy for P. canaliculata (AUC = 0.880). papers.title: Stabilizing a fragile antibiotic order: reconstructing the development of EU policy on antimicrobial resistance
papers.authors: Nora Molinari, Judith Miggelbrink
papers.abstract: Displaying findings from a discourse and dispositif analysis, this article traces the emergence and evolution of European Union antimicrobial resistance (AMR) regulation, addressing a significant gap in medical sociology and social science research. We understand antibiotics as infrastructure. Hence, we understand AMR as a phenomenon of infrastructural destabilization of a techno-social order and its political regulation as an endeavour to reestablish stability. The EU’s biopolitical regulatory dilemma — balancing its public health mandate versus economic imperatives and the individual’s right to access antibiotics — reflects deeper tensions between free trade market policies, extractive prosperity models, and the pursuit of technological control. While early regulatory steps were taken, the EU’s approach remains hesitant and fragmented, as the cultural symbolism of antibiotics as a “miracle weapon” and productivity factor obstructs recognition of AMR as a socially produced consequence. Ultimately, EU measures have prioritized status quo containment over structural reform, perpetuating an unstable antibiotic order.

papers.title: Restoration decisions in highly variable systems: Whether, when, and how to enhance kelp
papers.authors: Mei Z. Blundell, Marissa L. Baskett
papers.abstract: In highly variable ecosystems, natural variability can obscure signals of decline that warrant intervention, as there is often a lack of long-term data needed to distinguish between declines that are transient and likely to recover naturally and those that would be permanent without intervention. Implementing restoration for a species involves deciding on a threshold condition at which to intervene, duration that this threshold needs to be met before intervening, life stages at introduction, and amounts to introduce. Current bull and giant kelp restoration efforts in California were spurred by persistent kelp loss that started in 2013 following a disease outbreak among predators of the primary herbivore and a marine heatwave. We asked how decisions about intervention cue, threshold, wait time, life stage at introduction, and amount affect population outcomes against a backdrop of environmental variability. We analyzed additional context-dependencies on grazing and climate intensity. papers.title: Prevention of Destructive Fishing in the Waters of Tual City: Effective Surveillance and Law Enforcement Strategies
papers.authors: Suharta ., Sigit Bintoro, Riyan Maulana, Ismi Isti Anah
papers.source: Crossref / International Journal of Multidisciplinary Research and Growth Evaluation
papers.abstract: <jats:p>Destructive fishing in the waters of Tual City remains a significant environmental and socio-economic issue, threatening marine biodiversity and the livelihoods of local fishermen. This study analyzes the problem using a SWOT approach, identifying strengths such as existing government regulations and rich marine resources, weaknesses including limited enforcement capacity and economic dependence on harmful fishing practices, opportunities such as growing global demand for sustainable seafood, and threats like illegal fishing and climate change. Based on the SWOT analysis, several policy recommendations are proposed, including strengthening law enforcement, promoting sustainable alternative livelihoods, enhancing education and awareness programs, expanding marine protected areas (MPAs), and creating market incentives for responsible fisheries. These strategies aim to transition Tual City towards sustainable fisheries management, balancing environmental conservation with economic development. Effective implementation of these policies will not only mitigate destructive fishing but also ensure long-term resilience for both the ecosystem and local fishing communities.</jats:p>

papers.title: Microplastics and forest fungi: a review and call for comprehensive research
papers.authors: Toktam Farzaneh, Christian Laforsch, Claus Bässler
papers.abstract: Abstract Fungi are the main drivers of the global carbon and nutrient cycle and act as ecosystem engineers in forest ecosystems by regulating primary production and decomposition. Moreover, fungi are among the most diverse organisms in forest ecosystems and affect almost all forest microhabitats, from the canopy to the soil. In contrast to aquatic and agricultural ecosystems, forest ecosystems have received less attention in assessing the effects of microplastic pollution on biodiversity and ecosystem functioning. However, a recent study demonstrated that airborne microplastics are present even in remote forests, averaging 11.9 ± 7.1 particles m⁻³ of air. Thus, we summarize our current understanding of how microplastics enter forests and move within these ecosystems to assess potential risks to diverse fungal habitats. Next, we summarize the state of the art concerning how microplastics affect fungal individuals, fungal diversity, and related ecosystem processes. papers.abstract: The papaya mealybug, Paracoccus marginatus Williams and Granara de Willink (Hemiptera: Pseudococcidae), is an economically important invasive pest with a broad host range. Biological control, particularly through the encyrtid parasitoid Acerophagus papayae, has considerable potential for suppressing populations of this pest. The present investigation evaluated the life-table and age-specific fecundity parameters of A. papayae developing on P. marginatus during 2020–21 and 2021–22. Cohorts were followed from emergence until death, and age-specific survival and fecundity data were used to estimate major population and reproductive parameters. papers.title: Stage-wise collaborative feature enhancement for accurate maize insect pest detection in complex agricultural scenes
papers.authors: Jiayi Zuo, Cong Zhang, 冬寒 刘, Zheng Wang
papers.abstract: Introduction Accurate maize pest detection is hindered by morphological similarity among pest categories, complex backgrounds, and the loss of spatial detail in small targets Methods To address these challenges, we developed a stage-wise collaborative feature enhancement framework based on RT-DETR-R18. A Similarity-aware Decoupling Module combines orthogonal feature transformation with channel excitation to enhance discriminative backbone features. Adaptive Sparse Self-Attention regulates high-level inter-region interactions, whereas an Efficient Up-Convolution Block recovers spatial detail during top-down feature fusion. The method was evaluated on a primary dataset comprising 2,311 images from four maize pest categories and on the separately constructed IP102-Maize dataset, which was derived from the public IP102 benchmark and comprised 4,533 images from 13 categories. Results On the primary dataset, the proposed method achieved 90.4% mAP@50 and 67.9% mAP@50:95, improving mAP@50 by 2.7 percentage points over RT-DETR-R18. The model contained 20.9 M parameters and required 58.9 GFLOPs. On IP102-Maize, it achieved 64.1% mAP@50, exceeding RT-DETR-R18, RT-DETR-R34, and YOLOv10-S by 2.

papers.title: Sustaining the Third Pole (Himalayas): Artificial intelligence and blockchain for climate actions
papers.authors: Harsh Kumar Chauhan
papers.abstract: The Himalayas, often known as the 'Third Pole' or 'Water Tower of Asia', are vital for the water security of millions residing in the Asian continent. The region is facing a number of ecological, environmental, and social challenges, such as climate change, biodiversity loss, pollution, and border disputes. Conventional strategies for addressing these challenges have mostly failed to yield satisfactory outcomes. The present study examines the challenges being faced by the Himalayan region. It also explores the potential of AI (Artificial Intelligence) and BT (Blockchain Technology) in solving these challenges by suggesting a conceptual framework for integrating AI and BT to deliver sustainable outcomes in the region. This framework is the multi-stage integration of AI-generated data and BT secure governance mechanism for transboundary climate action. AI offers advanced capabilities for data collection, climate modeling, disaster prediction, and monitoring of biodiversity and ecosystems in the Himalayas. Methods: In June 2016, a total of 30 toxic element samples were taken from surface soils to examine their contents of lead (Pb), Zinc (Zn), Copper (Cu), Nickel (Ni), Arsenic (As), Chromium (Cr), and Cadmium (Cd). papers.abstract: Campylobacter is a constant concern in ensuring food safety, as it is one of the most common pathogens in food. The main source of Campylobacter species in food is poultry meat, and the primary production of this meat is a critical point where measures need to be taken to reduce its presence in the food chain. Therefore, poultry slaughterhouses are recognized as places where it is necessary to implement measures to control and reduce the number of Campylobacter spp. Food business operators are obliged to ensure greater hygiene on the slaughter line, through the inspection of equipment for each step of slaughter and the application of regular cleaning protocols. Continuous monitoring of the presence and abundance of Campylobacter spp. on the slaughter line provides data on the validity of hygiene control measures in the slaughterhouse, as well as the data needed to assess the microbiological risk in poultry meat. Monitoring the presence of Campylobacter spp. in poultry slaughterhouses is a basic activity that is necessary for taking measures to reduce contamination, improve microbiological safety in poultry processing and thus improve the food safety system as a whole. papers.abstract: Cashew gummosis is an emerging phytopathological threat showing an expanding distribution across Côte dʹIvoire. Elucidating the primary etiological agent is a critical prerequisite for developing targeted disease management strategies. To this end, a total of 105 fungal isolates comprising the genera Lasiodiplodia, Pestalotia, and Ceratocystis, which were recovered from symptomatic gummosis lesions were evaluated.Two distinct inoculation protocols were used: mechanically wounded and non-wounded cortical tissue applications. The bioassays showed that macroscopic symptoms developed exclusively following the wounded inoculation protocol, confirming that structural tissue compromise was necessary for fungal entry. Furthermore, symptoms typical of gummosis were confined to seedlings inoculated with Lasiodiplodia isolates. Successful re-isolation of the fungus from newly induced lesions satisfied Koch’s postulates, confirming that this genus is the causative agent of cashew gummosis in Côte dʹIvoire. Given the global impact of mycotoxins on food safety and animal health, this study addresses an urgent issue in agricultural science. It highlights the various environmental, physical, and biological factors influencing mycotoxin production, providing valuable insights for developing effective management strategies. The study also discusses the health risks associated with specific mycotoxins, such as zearalenone and fumonisins, which have been linked to serious health issues in both animals and humans. Furthermore, it emphasizes the need for ongoing prevention and control programs to mitigate mycotoxin contamination in the food chain. By exploring analytical challenges and proposing future directions for research and policy, this work contributes significantly to the understanding of mycotoxin dynamics in agricultural systems. papers.abstract: <jats:p>Background: Minimally invasive coronary artery bypass grafting (MICS CABG) via left anterior thoracotomy has emerged as a less invasive alternative to conventional open sternotomy (OPEN CABG), offering potential benefits in perioperative outcomes and complication rates. Objective. The aim of this study was to compare procedural characteristics, ventilation duration, drainage volumes, and postoperative complications between MICS CABG and OPEN CABG in a single-center cohort in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Methods. This retrospective cross-sectional study included 262 patients who underwent surgical revascularization between January 2019 and June 2023. Results. MICS CABG was associated with a shorter median procedure time (2.5 vs. 3.5 hours, p<0.001) and reduced mechanical ventilation duration (11.0 vs. 14.0 hours, p<0.001). papers.abstract: Abstract Plant disease recognition under real-field scenarios is still a challenging task because of high variations in terms of symptom presentation, affected plant organs, lighting, background, and severity of diseases. Existing deep learning methods typically utilize single feature representation or fixed ensemble strategies that limits their ability for adaptation to heterogeneous disease manifestations. In addition, existing durian disease classification studies have mainly focused on organ-specific recognition, such as leaf or trunk disease classification, whereas real-field disease recognition requires handling diverse manifestations across different plant organs and visual conditions. These limitations highlight the need for an adaptive framework that can exploit complementary representations from heterogeneous architectures while dynamically determining their relevance for each input sample. Motivated by these challenges, This study proposes Reliability-Aware Cross-Expert Gating Network (RACEGNet) for durian disease classification. papers.abstract: Introduction The use of distributed sensing infrastructures is increasingly becoming a key approach to environmental monitoring that is required to be mobile, flexible and adaptable to non-stationary conditions, preserve data privacy and consume as few resources as possible. The decentralized training paradigm provided by Federated Learning together with the ability of adapting sequentially over time without forgetting from Continual Learning has resulted in a concept of Federated Continual Learning (FCL) which offers a promising approach for privacy preserving environmental sensing systems that are capable of learning over time without forgetting. This systematic review provides an in-depth synthesis of the latest research, progress, environmental applications, sustainability, trustworthiness and future directions of Federated Continual Learning (FCL) for environmental monitoring. papers.title: PrinTE: a forward simulation framework for studying the role of transposable elements in genome expansion and contraction
papers.authors: Christopher W. Benson, Ting-Hsuan Chen, Susan J. Thomson, Cecilia Hong Deng, Shujun Ou
papers.abstract: Abstract Genome expansion and contraction are driven by transposable element activity, but the underlying dynamics remain enigmatic due to a lack of historical records tracing these changes. Here, we present PrinTE, a forward-time simulator of whole-genome sequences with customizable transposon dynamics for identifying the evolutionary parameters most consistent with an observed genome. Across simulations spanning four orders of magnitude, PrinTE recovers transposon insertion and deletion rates with less than 6% error. We demonstrate PrinTE on Arabidopsis and the fungal subdivision Pucciniomycotina, including myrtle rust ( Austropuccinia psidii ), which expanded its genome size to 1,018 Mb through transposon amplifications. Our simulations show that recombination-based removal of LTR retrotransposons alone cannot prevent genome obesity, and that preventing their invasion in the first place is more effective. We hypothesize that A. psidii might have experienced a prolonged expansion phase followed by a potent and ongoing period of contraction.

papers.abstract: Background Ferroptosis is a regulated form of cell death driven by iron-dependent lipid peroxidation and oxidative stress. It has emerged as a key contributor to the pathophysiology of cancer, neurodegenerative disorders, and cardiovascular diseases. Coumarins, a diverse class of benzopyrone-derived compounds, exhibit antioxidant, pro-oxidant, and iron-chelating properties, suggesting their potential role in modulating ferroptotic pathways. Aim This review aims to systematically evaluate the role of certain coumarins as modulators of ferroptosis and to explore their therapeutic implications across major disease contexts. Methods A comprehensive literature analysis was conducted focusing on experimental and preclinical studies investigating the interaction between coumarins and ferroptosis-related mechanisms, including iron metabolism, lipid peroxidation, and antioxidant defense systems such as the GPX4/GSH axis. Results Available preclinical evidence indicates that coumarins exert dual regulatory effects on ferroptosis. papers.title: Genome-wide and haplotype mapping reveals genetic drivers of biomass productivity per unit water and nitrogen in sorghum
papers.authors: Pramod Ramchandra Sargar, Niranjan Ravindra Thakur, Shivaji Mehtre, Pradeep Ruperao, Christian Hermans
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Improving crop productivity per unit of water and nitrogen is central to climate resilient sorghum improvement, yet the genetic architecture of biomass-based resource productivity remains poorly resolved across contrasting production environments. This study integrated multi-environment phenotyping with 1.75 million SNPs derived from whole genome resequencing of 172 cultivated Sorghum bicolor and S. bicolor × S. halepense derivative lines evaluated across temperate Mediterranean and semi-arid tropical environments. Results Biomass-based water productivity and partial factor productivity of applied nitrogen displayed extensive genetic variation and high broad-sense heritability of 0.75 to 0.81, whereas grain-based indices were more strongly influenced by genotype × environment interaction. Multi-model genome wide association analyses identified 27 significant SNPs defining 22 genomic regions for biomass-based productivity. papers.title: Tracking Plum Curculio (Coleoptera: Curculionidae) Movement in Blueberry and Peach Fields Using Protein Immunomarkers
papers.authors: Timothy P Lampasona, Cesar Rodriguez‐Saona, Anne L. Nielsen
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Plum curculio, Conotrachelus nenuphar (Herbst), is a native fruit pest. Adults emerge from overwintering sites in wooded areas and disperse into crop fields in the spring. However, their movement patterns within fields after this initial dispersal remain poorly understood. In this study, we used protein markers to investigate the in‐field dispersal of C. nenuphar adults in peach ( Prunus persica L.) and highbush blueberry ( Vaccinium corymbosum L.) fields. Chicken egg albumin (egg whites) was applied along field borders and bovine casein (cow's milk) within field interiors. Adults were collected daily using beat sampling, and enzyme‐linked immunosorbent assays (ELISA) were used to detect egg and/or milk proteins on individual insects. This approach provided a form of behavioural forensics, allowing us to trace each insect's movement within the field. Results indicated a strong edge effect in both crops, with 64.3% and 78.0% of adults collected along the border in blueberry and peach, respectively. papers.title: Optimal Control Analysis and Cost‐Effectiveness Calculations of Chickenpox Transmission Dynamics
papers.authors: Ahuod S. Alsheri, Hegagi Mohamed Ali, Essam M. Elsaid, Mohamed Rabea Eid, W. S. Hassanin
papers.source: OpenAlex / Optimal Control Applications and Methods
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This study develops and analyses a mathematical model for chickenpox transmission dynamics. The model's basic properties, including positivity, boundedness, and stability of disease‐free and endemic equilibria, are rigorously established. The basic reproduction number is derived, and sensitivity analysis identifies the most sensitive parameters. An optimal control problem is formulated with four time‐dependent controls (preventive measures, vaccination, pharmaceutical interventions, and non‐pharmaceutical treatments). Numerical simulations using a forward‐backward sweep method (FBSM) are conducted. Several control scenarios that resulted from the intersection of the recommended controls to clarify the impact of these controls and explore the most effective way to halt the disease's progress are presented. Moreover, the cost‐effectiveness analysis is presented to offer a quantitative comparison between the suggested five control scenarios. papers.authors: Dušan Adamov, Milica Vranešević, Dragana Stamenov, Simonida Đurić
papers.abstract: Abstract Soil is a non-renewable natural resource essential for supporting plants, animals, and microorganisms. The intensification of conventional agriculture has substantially affected soil health, including its microbial component. This review evaluates how sustainable agricultural practices, including crop rotation, intercropping, cover cropping, organic amendments, and agroforestry, influence microbial aspects of soil health, with particular emphasis on microbial biomass, diversity, community composition, and functions related to nutrient cycling. Peer-reviewed studies published up to 2025 were identified through Web of Science, PubMed, and Google Scholar using combinations of terms describing individual agricultural practices and microbial soil health parameters. The reviewed evidence indicates that crop diversification can enhance microbial biomass and modify microbial community composition through changes in soil properties, nutrient cycling, root exudation, and organic inputs, although responses vary among cropping systems and environmental conditions. papers.authors: Tinatin Doolotkeldieva, Батма Жусупова
papers.abstract: Schrenk’s spruce ( Picea schrenkiana ) is a dominant coniferous tree species in the Western Tian Shan forests and plays an important ecological role in maintaining mountain forest ecosystems in Kyrgyzstan. In recent years, the Sary-Chelek Biosphere Reserve has seen a significant increase in diseased and declining spruce trees, raising concerns about forest health and ecosystem stability. The present study aimed to investigate the fungal communities associated with diseased roots, stems, and needles of Schrenk’s spruce in the Sary-Chelek Biosphere Reserve, Kyrgyzstan. We identified fungal isolates from symptomatic plant tissues using morphological characteristics, ITS (5.8S rRNA) sequencing, and species-specific molecular markers. Mycological analysis revealed a diverse fungal community associated with diseased spruce tissues. Penicillium and Talaromyces species were predominantly isolated from infected roots. papers.authors: Joseph Abazaami
papers.abstract: Abstract Food security and climate resilience sit in uncomfortable tension across sub-Saharan Africa, and climate-smart agriculture (CSA) has been promoted as the bridge between them. Whether participatory action research (PAR) interventions can close the knowledge-to-practice gap in a lasting way remains inadequately answered in West African smallholder contexts. This paper presents findings from the end-of-project evaluation of the ReDIAL project, a four-year (2020–2024) EU-funded initiative across five agroecologically diverse districts in Ghana. The evaluation used a convergent parallel mixed-methods design: 400 household surveys, 50 focus group discussions, and 60 key informant interviews. By endline, 96% of project beneficiaries had received CSA training and roughly nine in ten were actively applying at least one CSA practice on their farms. Village Savings and Loan Associations (VSLAs) proved central—not as peripheral financial add-ons, but as the institutional mechanism that converted knowledge into sustained practice by providing farmers the credit needed to act on what they had learned. papers.abstract: Abstract Background Bryozoans are ancient colonial animals that have existed for over 470 million years and are widely distributed across aquatic environments. Recently, many spherical colloids (average diameter≈1 meter in diameter), containing bryozoans and diverse microorganisms, were found in the Hanjiang river in China. In this study, we investigated these bryozoan-dominated microbial complexes using metagenomic sequencing, metabolomic profiling, and complementary approaches. Results The results revealed that the microbial structure dominated by bryozoans included eukaryotes such as fungi, microalgae, as well as prokaryotes such as bacteria, and acellular entities such as viruses. All members form a highly integrated consortium that collaboratively maintains community function and stability, which displayed the shape and structure of a regular microbial complex and increased in size. papers.authors: José Luis Ruiz, Bárbara Díaz-Terenti, Thierry Léfèvre, Rakiswendé Serge Yerbanga, Thomas D. Otto
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT To survive and multiply in different host niches, malaria parasites require sets of proteins that are expressed during the life cycle in a timely manner. Plasmodium malariae is a human malaria parasite that is present in most malaria-endemic regions. However, this species remains enigmatic because it is very challenging to culture, its low parasitaemia in human infections, and frequent co-infection with other malarias. We investigate the transcriptome of P. malariae during transmission in the vector by analyzing RNA-seq data from midgut and salivary gland parasite stages obtained in two experimental mosquito infections with field P. malariae isolates. We detected unique expression patterns of the ApiAP2 family of transcription factors, many of which appear to function as master regulators during sporogony. papers.abstract: Abstract Koalas are now under threat of extinction from anthropological environmental change and the impacts of koala retrovirus (KoRV) induced immunosuppression and chlamydiosis, with these disease and environmental threats potentially interconnected through the effects of physiological stress. In this study, we investigated the associations among glucocorticoid metabolites (FGMs: cortisol, corticosterone and tetrahydrocortisol), KoRV load, chlamydiosis and two koala herpes viruses (PcGHV-1 and 2) across a landscape gradient of human modification/activity on the mid-north coast of NSW, Australia. Contrary to previous studies, FGM levels were not significantly correlated with any disease measures, which may be related to small sample sizes and baseline differences between individuals in hormone concentrations due to proposed intrinsic and extrinsic factors identified here. papers.authors: Hao Zheng, Jie Yin, Yang Yang, Yide Yang, Guanghe Wang
papers.abstract: Infections with Ralstonia solanacearum have caused considerable agricultural and economic losses. Complex interactions among pathogens, the soil microbiome and soil properties determine health status; however, their interactions have not been explored thoroughly. Here, we collected soils from local naturally healthy and diseased tobacco fields, used Illumina amplicon sequencing to analyze the soil microbial community, determined the physicochemical properties of the soils, and explored the disease-suppressive mechanism of the healthy soil. We found that the microbial structure significantly differed and that the microbial network was more complex in healthy soils than in diseased soils. The key indicator species of the microbial community are also different; those of healthy soil included Sphingomonas and Pseudomonas , which are potentially beneficial bacteria. papers.authors: Tianyi Ren, Manoj Kandoth, Paul Galpern
papers.abstract: Non-crop habitats can serve as reservoirs for beneficial ground beetles (Coleoptera: Carabidae), potentially shaping their distribution and community compositions in adjacent croplands. These edge-related changes in carabid communities can influence multiple ecosystem services, including weed seed predation. The extent to which proximity to these habitats shapes carabid distributions and seed predation services within large fields and prairie ecosystems remains relatively understudied. Within the carabid communities, the foraging and movement response of smaller granivores to larger omnivores may further influence edge-related distribution patterns and weed seed predation services. In this study, we deployed seed cards with pitfall traps at sampling stations across 10 fields to investigate these relationships in Alberta, Canada. We found edge effect over a long-distance gradient for seed predation intensity, and for omnivorous carabids, but not for granivorous species. papers.authors: Chaojie Wang, Bowen Tian, Meike Liu, Longyan Chen, Ping Wang
papers.abstract: Lepturinae is the third largest subfamily of the longhorn beetle family (Cerambycidae), however its phylogenetic relationships remain unclear. To address this, we sequenced and annotated the complete mitogenomes of Grammoptera (Neoencyclops) paucula and Encyclops hubeiensis, which were 16,095 bp and 16,448 bp in length, respectively. Each mitogenome contained 37 genes, including 13 protein-coding genes (PCGs), 22 transfer RNAs (tRNAs), two ribosomal RNAs (rRNAs), and a control region. Phylogenetic trees reconstructed from the 13 mitochondrial PCGs and their corresponding amino acid sequences datasets further clarified the evolutionary relationships within Lepturinae and resolved the phylogenetic relationships among its tribes.
